source_text: Δύνασαι καὶ τῶν χρημάτων ἐπίπροσθεν εἶναι; φράσον καὶ οὐκ ἀπάγει σε Χριστὸς τῆς κτήσεως, ὁ κύριος οὐ φθονεῖ. ἀλλ᾿ ὁρᾷς σεαυτὸν ἡττώμενον ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν καὶ ἀνατρεπόμενον; ἄφες. ῥῖψον. μίσησον, ἀπόταξαι, φύγε· »κἂν ὁ δέξιός σου ὀφθαλμὸς σκανδαλίζῃ σε. ταχέως ἔκκοψον αὐτόν·« αἱρετώτερον ἑτεροφθάλμῳ βασιλεία θεοῦ ἢ ὁλοκλήρῳ τὸ πῦρ· κἂν χεὶρ κἂν ποὺς κἂν ἡ ψυχή, μίσησον αὐτήν. ἂν γὰρ ἐνταῦθα ἀπόληται ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, ἐκεῖ σωθήσεται.
thought_title: Wealth must be renounced only when it defeats you
orientation: Clement is addressing the rich believer directly, continuing his argument that possessions themselves are not condemned, but only the soul's defeat by them.
pass_a_gloss: Are you able to be above [your] money? Say so, and Christ does not lead you away from [your] possession; the Lord does not begrudge. But do you see yourself being defeated by them and overturned? Let go. Throw away. Hate, renounce, flee. "Even if your right eye causes you to stumble, quickly cut it out." More choice [is] the kingdom of God for a one-eyed person than the fire for a whole [person]. Even if a hand, even if a foot, even if the soul, hate it. For if here it is destroyed for Christ's sake, there it will be saved.

choices.why: The spatial metaphor of standing over or above wealth captures Clement's point that the rich person may possess without being possessed; 'above' keeps the literal force of the preposition.
The verb means to be turned upside down or capsized; 'overturned' preserves the violent, physical image of the soul being wrecked by possessions.
The verb means to formally take leave of or bid farewell to; 'renounce' matches the glossary's ascetic register and the command's finality.
The adjective means having one eye; rendering it as a noun phrase keeps the contrast with 'whole person' clear and avoids the clinical 'monocular.'
The adjective means complete or intact in all parts; 'whole person' preserves the contrast with the mutilated one-eyed person and avoids implying moral wholeness.

pass_b_english: Can you stand above your money? Then say so. Christ does not drag you away from what you own, and the Lord does not begrudge you. But do you see yourself being defeated by your possessions and overturned by them? Then let them go. Throw them away. Hate them, renounce them, flee from them. "If your right eye causes you to stumble, cut it out quickly" (Mark 9:47). It is better to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to be thrown into the fire with both eyes intact. And if it is your hand, or your foot, or even your very soul—hate it. For if it is destroyed here for Christ's sake, it will be saved there.

problems.quote: "If your right eye causes you to stumble, cut it out quickly" (Matthew 5:29)
problems.source_quote: κἂν ὁ δέξιός σου ὀφθαλμὸς σκανδαλίζῃ σε. ταχέως ἔκκοψον αὐτόν
problems.why: Clement's wording (ταχέως, singular) matches Mark 9:43-47, not Matthew 5:29 which has βλέπεται and plural.
problems.fix: "If your right eye causes you to stumble, cut it out quickly" (Mark 9:47)
problems.ruling: Greek 'ταχέως ἔκκοψον αὐτὸν' not in Matthew 5:29; matches Mark 9:43‑47 style, so citation is wrong.

fixed: Changed citation from Matthew 5:29 to Mark 9:47 because Clement's wording (ταχέως, singular) matches Mark 9:43-47, not Matthew 5:29.

last_rejected.why: Source says 'cut it off' (ἔκκοψον), not 'cut it out'; wrong verb sense for eye removal.
last_rejected.ruling: ἔκκοψον = cut off; “cut it out” conveys same literal removal, not a meaning change.
